claimChanges.claimText: Oxford’s public AI Competency Centre tool guide lists ChatGPT Edu as a University SSO platform with a Confidential TPSA rating. Standard access is listed as free; Microsoft 365 Copilot and Google Gemini Pro are separate paid products. The guide has moved to OxIntranet and is no longer maintained; check successor guidance for current terms. Tool access is not assessment permission.

Oxford’s public AI Competency Centre tool guide lists Codex as a University SSO platform with a Confidential TPSA rating. Standard access is listed as free; Microsoft 365 Copilot and Google Gemini Pro are separate paid products. The guide has moved to OxIntranet and is no longer maintained; check successor guidance for current terms. Tool access is not assessment permission.

Oxford’s public AI Competency Centre tool guide lists Google Gemini as a University SSO platform with a Confidential TPSA rating. Standard access is listed as free; Microsoft 365 Copilot and Google Gemini Pro are separate paid products. The guide has moved to OxIntranet and is no longer maintained; check successor guidance for current terms. Tool access is not assessment permission.

Oxford’s public AI Competency Centre tool guide lists Microsoft Copilot Chat as a University SSO platform with a Confidential TPSA rating. Standard access is listed as free; Microsoft 365 Copilot and Google Gemini Pro are separate paid products. The guide has moved to OxIntranet and is no longer maintained; check successor guidance for current terms. Tool access is not assessment permission.

Staff setting summative assessment must: declare whether/how students can use AI; review assessment design for alignment with permitted AI use; ensure equality of baseline AI tool provision where authorised; specify declaration forms for student AI use; only identify suspected unauthorised AI use through marking or university-endorsed detection tools (the public page says none had received endorsement at its last update); and handle misconduct under usual disciplinary regulations.

MPLS guidance for DPhil and MSc by Research summative assessment requires a statement on GenAI use in the final thesis for submissions from Trinity Term 2026. The statement goes immediately after the abstract and covers compliance, uses and referencing. This is MPLS guidance, not proof of an identical rule in every division.

Students undertaking summative assessment must: complete assessment in line with the AI use declaration for each assignment; acknowledge their AI use via a formal declaration in the prescribed format; and understand that submitting work breaching AI specifications constitutes cheating and may constitute plagiarism, handled under usual disciplinary regulations.

The University's policy on AI use in summative assessment is based on three principles endorsed by Education Committee in Trinity term 2025: (1) educational practice must be grounded in values of integrity, honesty and transparency, which must be clearly articulated and frequently discussed; (2) every discrete unit of assessment must be carefully designed to be fit for its specific purposes, clearly articulated to students; (3) every summative assessment must be accompanied by a clear explanation of what appropriate assistance is permitted and what is forbidden, specifying how students should report assistance received.

The former Oxford public Information Security URL cited for cloud-AI security assessment now says the content has moved. The earlier recorded guidance is historical and is not current approval or prohibition. Consult successor Cyber Security/OxIntranet guidance; current detailed conditions could not be independently retrieved.

The public Oxford AI Competency Centre guide lists ChatGPT Edu, Codex, Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot Chat with Confidential TPSA ratings and University SSO. It now states that the public guide is no longer maintained and points to successor University guidance. This does not approve GitHub Copilot or personal consumer accounts.

MPLS postgraduate research guidance prohibits substantive AI-written thesis content, including close paraphrases, and producing plots or data visualisations directly from prompts. It distinguishes refining plotting code from generating research results. Confidential/private data use remains subject to applicable University data rules and approved institutional services.

The former Oxford public Information Security URL cited for external custom GPT use now says the content has moved. The earlier recorded guidance is historical and is not current approval or prohibition. Consult successor Cyber Security/OxIntranet guidance; current detailed conditions could not be independently retrieved.

The former Oxford public Information Security URL cited for AI transcription bots now says the content has moved. The earlier recorded guidance is historical and is not current approval or prohibition. Consult successor Cyber Security/OxIntranet guidance; current detailed conditions could not be independently retrieved.

For MPLS postgraduate research summative assessment, local editing and debugging tools are permitted without declaration. Background research, translation, bibliography indexes and general understanding are allowed without declaration. AI coding is permitted when it serves a research purpose and is not the substantive project output; students remain responsible for correctness and should declare AI-generated code, excluding debugging.

Oxford’s public summative-assessment policy says work breaching the assignment’s AI specifications constitutes cheating and may constitute plagiarism; suspected misuse is handled under usual disciplinary regulations and processes. It does not establish an AI-specific penalty.

Oxford’s research policy says users of a discrete GenAI tool should declare substantive use in their work. Where relevant they must make prompts and outputs available under open research principles. Its scope defines exclusions for certain assistance tasks; assessment research must also meet summative-assessment rules.

claimChanges.claimText: AWS Bedrock via Harvard API Platform is available through Harvard's API Platform for eligible users. The platform offers self-service AI API access, including pay-as-you-go or limited-access credit-redemption options; some individual APIs have limited eligibility stated in their documentation. API/developer services are approved up to Level 3 confidential data. Account access is separate from course, research-use and feature-specific approval.

Harvard-managed ChatGPT Edu is available by request at a monthly cost, with School or Unit approval and the service's listed eligibility. Codex is included with Harvard ChatGPT Edu licences. ChatGPT Chat and Codex are approved up to Level 3 confidential data; ChatGPT Work requires active monitoring of autonomous sessions for that data level. API keys require separate API Platform access, and connectors require security/privacy approval. Institutional access does not grant assessment permission.

Harvard Claude is available in paid Standard and Premium tiers, with requests reviewed and approved by Schools and Units. Licences include Chat, Code, Cowork and Science; API keys use a separate API Platform path. Chat and Code are approved up to Level 3 confidential data; Cowork requires active monitoring of autonomous sessions. Connectors require security/privacy approval. Tool access does not grant assessment permission.

Harvard-managed ChatGPT Edu is available by request at a monthly cost, with School or Unit approval and the service's listed eligibility. Codex is included with Harvard ChatGPT Edu licences. ChatGPT Chat and Codex are approved up to Level 3 confidential data; ChatGPT Work requires active monitoring of autonomous sessions for that data level. API keys require separate API Platform access, and connectors require security/privacy approval. Institutional access does not grant assessment permission.

Google Gemini (Basic) is included in Harvard's Basic Google Workspace tier for eligible account holders. Gemini Notebook is the current name of NotebookLM; Pro includes expanded Notebook limits. HUIT lists specific eligible Schools and user groups, with local approval for some Google Workspace account requests. Standard Gemini products are approved up to Level 3 confidential data, while agent sessions require active monitoring and connectors require separate review. Access is separate from assessment permission.

Google Gemini (Pro) is included in Harvard's paid Google AI Pro for Education tier, available by request. Gemini Notebook is the current name of NotebookLM; Pro includes expanded Notebook limits. HUIT lists specific eligible Schools and user groups, with local approval for some Google Workspace account requests. Standard Gemini products are approved up to Level 3 confidential data, while agent sessions require active monitoring and connectors require separate review. Access is separate from assessment permission.

Google Gemini API via Harvard API Platform is available through Harvard's API Platform for eligible users. The platform offers self-service AI API access, including pay-as-you-go or limited-access credit-redemption options; some individual APIs have limited eligibility stated in their documentation. API/developer services are approved up to Level 3 confidential data. Account access is separate from course, research-use and feature-specific approval.

HUIT's feature comparison lists Workspace Studio with Google Gemini Basic. This is a Gemini feature entry, not a separate blanket tool licence. Basic Google Workspace access is free for eligible users; Google AI Pro for Education requires a request at additional cost. School/account eligibility and enabled-feature/connector approvals still apply. Tool access does not grant assessment permission.

HUIT's feature comparison lists Workspace Studio with Google Gemini Pro. This is a Gemini feature entry, not a separate blanket tool licence. Basic Google Workspace access is free for eligible users; Google AI Pro for Education requires a request at additional cost. School/account eligibility and enabled-feature/connector approvals still apply. Tool access does not grant assessment permission.

Harvard AI Sandbox is a free institutional multi-model service for the School/user groups listed on its service page. It is approved up to Level 3 confidential data and states that input data will not train vendor models. HGSE access to the Sandbox for course-content uploads is through individual courses; HMS access/training conditions are School-specific. Access does not grant assessment permission.

AI APIs and Developer Tools via Harvard API Platform is available through Harvard's API Platform for eligible users. The platform offers self-service AI API access, including pay-as-you-go or limited-access credit-redemption options; some individual APIs have limited eligibility stated in their documentation. API/developer services are approved up to Level 3 confidential data. Account access is separate from course, research-use and feature-specific approval.

Harvard Microsoft Copilot Chat is included at no extra cost for eligible Harvard Microsoft 365 users, who sign in with HarvardKey. The Premium tier is available by request at additional cost and includes Microsoft 365 application integration. The service lists School/user eligibility. Institutional access and Level 3 approval for named managed products do not grant assessment permission; meeting use and connector approvals have additional conditions.

Harvard Microsoft Copilot Chat is included at no extra cost for eligible Harvard Microsoft 365 users, who sign in with HarvardKey. The Premium tier is available by request at additional cost and includes Microsoft 365 application integration. The service lists School/user eligibility. Institutional access and Level 3 approval for named managed products do not grant assessment permission; meeting use and connector approvals have additional conditions.

Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM; Basic) is included in Harvard's Basic Google Workspace tier for eligible account holders. Gemini Notebook is the current name of NotebookLM; Pro includes expanded Notebook limits. HUIT lists specific eligible Schools and user groups, with local approval for some Google Workspace account requests. Standard Gemini products are approved up to Level 3 confidential data, while agent sessions require active monitoring and connectors require separate review. Access is separate from assessment permission.

Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM; Pro) is included in Harvard's paid Google AI Pro for Education tier, available by request. Gemini Notebook is the current name of NotebookLM; Pro includes expanded Notebook limits. HUIT lists specific eligible Schools and user groups, with local approval for some Google Workspace account requests. Standard Gemini products are approved up to Level 3 confidential data, while agent sessions require active monitoring and connectors require separate review. Access is separate from assessment permission.

OpenAI Direct via Harvard API Platform is available through Harvard's API Platform for eligible users. The platform offers self-service AI API access, including pay-as-you-go or limited-access credit-redemption options; some individual APIs have limited eligibility stated in their documentation. API/developer services are approved up to Level 3 confidential data. Account access is separate from course, research-use and feature-specific approval.

Harvard guidance says Level 2 and above confidential data should not be entered into publicly available generative AI tools and must only be entered into tools assessed and approved for that use. HUIT-listed managed general-use tools are approved up to Level 3 with a Harvard account and are not approved for Level 4. Separate HMS Level 4 research/development services require their own access and data-use conditions.

FAS Office of Undergraduate Education requires faculty to inform students of the policies governing generative AI use in class. It recommends posting the policy on Canvas. This communication requirement does not choose an AI permission policy for the course.

Harvard guidance requires vendor generative AI tools to be assessed for risk by Harvard Information Security and Data Privacy before use in Harvard work. Users considering tools not currently offered should contact HUIT before procurement. Enabled connectors and new features may need their own review.

Harvard meeting guidance says AI assistants should not be used except approved tools with contractual protections or applicable approved pilots/accommodations. Participants must be informed and all must consent before recording/transcription begins. The guidance says not to use assistants when participants object (with a disability-accommodation consultation route), and to disable them in meetings involving Level 3 or higher information. Summaries must be reviewed before limited sharing; retention and litigation holds also apply.
Harvard guidance says users are responsible for any content they publish or share that includes AI-generated material, which may be inaccurate, fabricated or copyrighted.

HGSE states that, unless the instructor specifies otherwise, using generative AI to create all or part of a course assignment and submit it as one’s own violates its Academic Integrity Policy. Permissible learning uses include clarification, brainstorming and contextual scenarios; students must discuss uncertain uses with the instructor before use.

For permitted GenAI use in HGSE assignments, students must acknowledge and document the tools used, prompts if applicable, and how outputs were integrated. Direct citations must use proper citation format.

HGSE forbids making personal recordings of course meetings, with or without AI integrations; students needing recordings should discuss them with the instructor. Uploading substantial course content is only allowed through the Harvard-approved AI Sandbox, accessed through individual courses. Assistive-technology AI use must be coordinated with the Office of Student Affairs.

FAS OUE guidance requires documented student permission before faculty put original student content into a generative AI tool and says students should be informed of the risks. Its page also contains a broad no-confidentiality statement. HUIT separately describes contractual privacy protections for approved managed services; that data approval does not waive FAS student-content consent or course rules.
HMS Academic and Research Integrity guidance says AI tools cannot be listed as authors on papers. Authors should be transparent about using AI tools and explain how the tools were used.

HUIT’s general-use comparison applies Level 3-or-below approval and no-vendor-training protection only when logged in with a Harvard account. It does not approve Level 4 data. HMS separately lists special-request Level 4 tools and a Level 2 ceiling for automated meeting assistants. Product access, data approval, DUA/sponsor limits and assessment permission must be checked separately.

HMS responsible-use guidance advises users to verify AI outputs, follow applicable faculty/student handbook rules, be transparent about acceptable use and cite AI contributions appropriately. It separately requires attention to confidential data, regulations, sponsor requirements and DUA restrictions; it does not establish assessment permission.

HMS lists AI Sandbox, Claude, ChatGPT Edu, Microsoft Copilot Premium, Firefly, HMS Azure AI, HUIT API Portal and Longwood Cluster with different eligibility, training, data levels and costs. HMS provides one of Claude, ChatGPT Edu or Copilot Premium per eligible person. HMS Azure AI is a Level 4 service for HMS IT/project developers, and Longwood is a separate Level 4 research environment; this is not blanket Level 4 access for ordinary students.

Harvard guidance recommends that faculty clearly communicate permitted AI uses, if any, in classes and academic work; students are encouraged to ask their instructors for clarification. The applicable School and course rules determine permission.

The Harvard Law Graduate Program permits AI queries to clarify exam-relevant concepts while studying, but prohibits queries about exam subject matter during the exam. Pre-writing AI text for incorporation into an exam is not permitted. Instructors may set different rules only when described in writing and communicated to all students. This applies to the Graduate Program policy, not all Harvard courses.

Social Studies prohibits generative or agentic AI assistance in submitted coursework, exams/quizzes and all thesis stages by default. Instructors may publish alternative syllabus rules but must require disclosure. Thesis exceptions are case-specific: obtain supervisor approval, submit the AI Policy Attestation request, and secure DUS approval by November 1 of senior year, or April 1 for off-cycle fall seniors. The AI Policy Attestation form is required in consultation with the supervisor at Prospectus submission and again in senior year. Thesis work cannot reuse AI-assisted work from another course merely because that course allowed it. These rules apply to Social Studies requirements.

Harvard’s Bok Center advises faculty that AI checkers are not currently reliable evidence and may over-identify AI use. Its guidance supports contextual inquiry into student understanding, revision history, timestamps and citations. This does not establish a university-wide ban on all detection or exam-control technologies.

HMS offers one selected managed AI tool per eligible user. Its Sandbox/premium tool rows specify Quad-based faculty, staff and MD/DMD students, with training and some course-based exceptions. Managed tools outside meetings have a Level 3 ceiling; automated meeting assistants have a Level 2 ceiling. HMS Azure AI and Longwood Cluster are separately requested Level 4 environments. DUA, regulatory and sponsor limits still apply even to data-approved tools; no tool is approved for Level 5.

Harvard’s API Platform provides eligible users with self-service AI APIs, pay-as-you-go and limited-access credit-redemption options. Some APIs have narrower eligibility stated in their documentation. Developer services are approved up to Level 3 data. General-use licences do not include API keys; agent/connector features have their own reviewed conditions. Access does not override research data or assessment restrictions.

claimChanges.claimText: Cambridge says examiners across undergraduate, taught-postgraduate and research-postgraduate programmes may not upload, copy or share student work with GenAI/LLMs or use them to analyse submissions and produce feedback. The source also prohibits sharing student IP/submissions without student permission because of uncertain storage/use. Examiners may use AI to support their own feedback writing, such as consolidating personal notes or rephrasing comments; this is not blanket permission to upload student work.

Google Gemini is included in Cambridge’s University Google Workspace core apps for staff and students. University-account access is distinct from permitted coursework, assessment and research data use.

Most Cambridge staff and students have a standard Microsoft licence with Copilot Chat access at no extra charge. Microsoft 365 application integration requires an additional paid licence; UIS currently lists approximately £300 per user/year and an A3 or A5 account for purchase. Institutional account access and commercial data protection do not grant assessment permission.

Most Cambridge staff and students have a standard Microsoft licence with Copilot Chat access at no extra charge. Microsoft 365 application integration requires an additional paid licence; UIS currently lists approximately £300 per user/year and an A3 or A5 account for purchase. Institutional account access and commercial data protection do not grant assessment permission.

Google NotebookLM is included in Cambridge’s University Google Workspace core apps for staff and students. University-account access is distinct from permitted coursework, assessment and research data use.

Cambridge’s staff administrative-use guidance recommends avoiding confidential, sensitive or personal data in GenAI unless warranted and consistent with the guidance. This document expressly excludes teaching, student learning/assessment, research, and College or other separate-entity business. It is not an unconditional privacy prohibition for all student AI use.

For staff administrative work, Cambridge recommends its licensed Copilot, Gemini and NotebookLM wherever practicable. Other licensed tools are not prohibited but must follow applicable procurement processes and any requisite DPIA/ISRA risk assessments. Within this administrative guidance, the public free versions of the named tools must not be used for University activities. These rules do not establish student assessment permission.

For University staff administrative work, Cambridge’s risk mitigations require human evaluation before using GenAI outputs and acknowledgement when AI makes a significant and unrevised contribution to substantive or impactful work, such as formal policies or strategic reports. The guidance excludes teaching, student learning/assessment and research; it does not impose this administrative requirement on all student coursework.

Cambridge broadly permits appropriate GenAI use for personal study, research and formative work, with nuanced Department, Faculty or College guidance controlling the context. Students should check local rules with staff; this is not blanket permission for summative assessments.

Cambridge’s staff administrative guidance requires consideration of the purpose for which personal data was collected and compatibility of proposed AI use. With exceptions such as academic research, it says repurposing personal data for another GenAI task is inappropriate. Its separate discussion of automated decisions affecting people requires ultimate human involvement. The document’s own teaching/research and separate-entity exclusions remain relevant.

Cambridge’s staff administrative guidance says inputs to the University’s licensed Copilot, Gemini and NotebookLM are not used to train those tools. Free/unlicensed tools may use input for training, which may not be lawful for personal data. This is an institutional-product protection, not a guarantee for consumer accounts or permission for a particular task.

Cambridge’s educational AI framework supports Triposes, Departments, Faculties and Colleges setting their own local allowances. It is an educational policy framework; its existence must not be interpreted as absence of all central assessment or research requirements.

Cambridge’s staff administrative guidance says that in the limited circumstances requiring a formal risk assessment, the University DPIA and ISRA processes are the relevant processes. This is not a requirement to perform both assessments for every AI use. Applicable procurement and acceptable-use conditions still apply within the document’s administrative scope.

Assignment-specific rules take precedence. Students must not generate raw submission/presentation content without an initial self-written base or automatically generate references from content; tools managing student-identified references remain allowed. Relevant issues include sensitive data, ownership, copyright, ethics, integrity and security. The framework says there is no distinct University GenAI research policy; that does not mean research has no AI-related rules.

Cambridge reports its existing Turnitin terms/EULA are extended until 30 July 2027 and no EULA change will be implemented in 2026/27. The notice says student/staff data has not been used to develop GenAI/LLMs and Turnitin has no current plan to use student essays that way; this is not an unlimited future contractual guarantee. Turnitin similarity screening is available under University course-use conditions, while Cambridge separately advises not relying on AI-authorship detectors as evidence.

A student using any unacknowledged content generated by artificial intelligence within a summative assessment as though it is their own work constitutes academic misconduct, unless explicitly stated otherwise in the assessment brief.

claimChanges.claimText: Google Gemini is officially licensed and provided to ETH Zurich employees and students free of charge through the ETH Google Workspace Cloud Subscription with enterprise data protection (no model training). CISO cloud assessment remains OPEN; Google tools are not approved for confidential or protected personal data. An optional fee-based Google AI Pro license is available for employees.

Microsoft Copilot is officially licensed for ETH Zurich. M365 Copilot Chat is available free to all members and approved for internal data. M365 Copilot Work mode without web search is approved for confidential data for licensed employees. Uploading strictly confidential data is prohibited.

Google NotebookLM is officially available free of charge to ETH Zurich members through the Google Workspace Cloud Subscription with enterprise data protection. CISO cloud assessment remains OPEN; tools lacking assessment have not been released for confidential or personal ETH data.
ETH Zurich advocates a proactive approach to the use of generative AI in educational contexts, emphasising responsible use among students and lecturers.

Students are responsible for the content of work they submit. Performance assessments must be conducted independently and personally; GenAI may serve a supplementary role but not replace student efforts.
Lecturers determine whether and how GenAI may be used in their courses and for respective assessments. Teaching materials created with GenAI must be subjected to quality control by the lecturer.

Violations of GenAI guidelines such as use of unauthorised aids or non-disclosure of their use are subject to disciplinary action under existing performance assessment rules and the declaration of originality.
ETH Zurich recommends Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, and NotebookLM for teaching purposes, as they offer data-protected access via ETH accounts where personal data is not used for training models.

Students must refrain from disclosing copyrighted, private, or confidential information to commercial GenAI clients unless expressly permitted, and must respect privacy and copyright of content they work with.

ETH Zurich's teaching guidelines instruct students to be transparent about their use of generative AI and to identify which tools contributed to which parts of their work, in accordance with applicable lecturer instructions and citation conventions. For scientific writing and theses, students should agree in advance with their supervisors on authorised AI use and disclosure requirements. ETH Library guidance recognises an exception where a supervisor has expressly agreed that particular AI use need not be separately declared. In the absence of such an agreement, undeclared use may constitute a breach of academic integrity.
ETH Zurich states that technical recognition of AI-generated output is currently unreliable and will probably remain so; trust in such methods is not appropriate.

ETH Zurich's declaration of originality provides two options: confirming that no generative AI was used, or confirming that authorised generative AI was used and its disclosure agreed with the supervisor. Bachelor's and Master's theses require a signed declaration of originality, while requirements for other written assessments depend on the applicable academic instructions. Doctoral candidates declare independent authorship through the doctoral examination registration process. The permitted use, disclosure format and any exceptions must follow the relevant supervisor and unit requirements.

ETH Zurich prohibits the processing of strictly confidential information in external cloud AI services. Confidential information may be processed only in services and configurations explicitly approved for that classification. ETH IT guidance distinguishes Microsoft 365 Copilot Work mode without web search, which is approved for confidential data, from Copilot Chat and web mode, which are approved for internal data. Unassessed AI services must not be used for confidential ETH data or protected personal data.

ETH Library guidance requires researchers to remain responsible for their scientific work and to verify AI-generated information, references and quotations. Generative AI tools cannot be listed as scientific authors or relied upon as authoritative scientific sources. Researchers should agree on permitted AI use with collaborators and follow applicable departmental, funder, publisher and journal requirements. Disclosure of an AI tool's contribution is distinct from citing that tool as evidence for a scientific claim.

ETH Library provides Turnitin Originality to eligible professors and lecturers for text-similarity checking, subject to data classification and responsible selective-use guidance. Only public or internal documents may be uploaded. Similarity screening is distinct from AI-authorship detection; ETH Zurich warns that technical detection of AI-generated output is unreliable and should not be treated as conclusive evidence.

claimChanges.claimText: Google Gemini is officially licensed and provided to ETH Zurich employees and students free of charge through the ETH Google Workspace Cloud Subscription with enterprise data protection (no model training). CISO cloud assessment remains OPEN; Google tools are not approved for confidential or protected personal data. An optional fee-based Google AI Pro license is available for employees.

Microsoft Copilot is officially licensed for ETH Zurich. M365 Copilot Chat is available free to all members and approved for internal data. M365 Copilot Work mode without web search is approved for confidential data for licensed employees. Uploading strictly confidential data is prohibited.

Google NotebookLM is officially available free of charge to ETH Zurich members through the Google Workspace Cloud Subscription with enterprise data protection. CISO cloud assessment remains OPEN; tools lacking assessment have not been released for confidential or personal ETH data.
ETH Zurich advocates a proactive approach to the use of generative AI in educational contexts, emphasising responsible use among students and lecturers.

Students are responsible for the content of work they submit. Performance assessments must be conducted independently and personally; GenAI may serve a supplementary role but not replace student efforts.
Lecturers determine whether and how GenAI may be used in their courses and for respective assessments. Teaching materials created with GenAI must be subjected to quality control by the lecturer.

Violations of GenAI guidelines such as use of unauthorised aids or non-disclosure of their use are subject to disciplinary action under existing performance assessment rules and the declaration of originality.
ETH Zurich recommends Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, and NotebookLM for teaching purposes, as they offer data-protected access via ETH accounts where personal data is not used for training models.

Students must refrain from disclosing copyrighted, private, or confidential information to commercial GenAI clients unless expressly permitted, and must respect privacy and copyright of content they work with.

ETH Zurich's teaching guidelines instruct students to be transparent about their use of generative AI and to identify which tools contributed to which parts of their work, in accordance with applicable lecturer instructions and citation conventions. For scientific writing and theses, students should agree in advance with their supervisors on authorised AI use and disclosure requirements. ETH Library guidance recognises an exception where a supervisor has expressly agreed that particular AI use need not be separately declared. In the absence of such an agreement, undeclared use may constitute a breach of academic integrity.
ETH Zurich states that technical recognition of AI-generated output is currently unreliable and will probably remain so; trust in such methods is not appropriate.

ETH Zurich's declaration of originality provides two options: confirming that no generative AI was used, or confirming that authorised generative AI was used and its disclosure agreed with the supervisor. Bachelor's and Master's theses require a signed declaration of originality, while requirements for other written assessments depend on the applicable academic instructions. Doctoral candidates declare independent authorship through the doctoral examination registration process. The permitted use, disclosure format and any exceptions must follow the relevant supervisor and unit requirements.

ETH Zurich prohibits the processing of strictly confidential information in external cloud AI services. Confidential information may be processed only in services and configurations explicitly approved for that classification. ETH IT guidance distinguishes Microsoft 365 Copilot Work mode without web search, which is approved for confidential data, from Copilot Chat and web mode, which are approved for internal data. Unassessed AI services must not be used for confidential ETH data or protected personal data.

ETH Library guidance requires researchers to remain responsible for their scientific work and to verify AI-generated information, references and quotations. Generative AI tools cannot be listed as scientific authors or relied upon as authoritative scientific sources. Researchers should agree on permitted AI use with collaborators and follow applicable departmental, funder, publisher and journal requirements. Disclosure of an AI tool's contribution is distinct from citing that tool as evidence for a scientific claim.

ETH Library provides Turnitin Originality to eligible professors and lecturers for text-similarity checking, subject to data classification and responsible selective-use guidance. Only public or internal documents may be uploaded. Similarity screening is distinct from AI-authorship detection; ETH Zurich warns that technical detection of AI-generated output is unreliable and should not be treated as conclusive evidence.

AI-Guide is an internal guidance and advisory productivity tool within NUS IT's AI-Know suite for staff workflows; general student access is unverified.

AI-Know is NUS IT's in-house enterprise AI platform and training suite, serving nearly 1,000 staff across 120+ departments; student expansion is planned on the horizon and partially mediated through specific applications.
AI-Minute is an automated meeting minutes generator within the AI-Know suite deployed for university administrative staff; general student access is unverified.

NUS policy states that verdicts of AI tools purporting to determine whether an input was generated by AI are not admissible as evidence in disciplinary processes to charge students with academic dishonesty or as justification to penalize student work.

NUS policy states that submitting AI-generated work without acknowledging AI use constitutes academic dishonesty and plagiarism, punishable under university disciplinary processes assuming the case can be made.

NUS policy recommends that instructors should be transparent about where and how they deploy AI in NUS courses, particularly when generating content, acting as virtual tutors, or aiding assessment feedback and grading.

NUS policy requires prior approval by Head of Department or Deanery under oversight of Chair of AI-COP, obtained via submission to the AI System for Assurance and Evaluation, before deploying AI to provide instruction, feedback, or marks. In general, except for AI marking of objective or closed-ended assessments, a human instructor or reviewer should remain in the loop, and spot checks should still be conducted even where scoring is considered reliable.

NUS policy sets the default assumption that AI tool use is permitted for unsupervised (take-home) assessments with due acknowledgement; if an assessment forbids AI for pedagogical reasons, crucial aspects of that assessment should be conducted in person and under instructor supervision.
NUS policy states that instructors should use NUS-approved AI tools whenever NUS data is involved, defining NUS data as information managed, protected, or controlled under university obligations.
NUS maintains an institutional Policy for Use of AI in Teaching and Learning (current version 15 Sept 2026), supplemented by Library Essentials guidelines infographics and THE1005 module resources.

NUS Libraries guidance instructs students to always check assignment guidelines for specific AI instructions and consult citation style guides and publisher policies when using AI in academic or published work.

Starting 31 August 2026, NUS provides all students, faculty, and staff with access to ChatGPT Edu in a university-managed environment where workspace conversations and data are excluded from training OpenAI models.

Starting from Academic Year 2026/27, NUS requires all incoming first-year undergraduate students to complete the compulsory foundational AI literacy module THE1008 Applied Generative AI: From Prompting to Evaluation.

NUS Libraries and NUS IT announced AI Sense Maker, a conversational AI literature discovery platform powered by OpenAI LLM scheduled to be officially launched on 20 August 2026, indexing over 150,000 institutional library assets.

NUS Press prohibits submitting manuscripts containing wording from AI models (including AI polishing/streamlining) and requires detailed tool declarations upon submission; AI images and diagrams are not accepted.
NUS Centre for Future-ready Graduates provides current students with CFG AI-Xplore, a virtual career advisory chatbot hosted on the AI-Know platform accessed via the AI-Create Marketplace tab.

NUS policy strictly prohibits sharing AI tool accounts under any circumstances; using a shared account may raise collusion concerns and, where misconduct is established, may result in disciplinary action.

claimChanges.claimText: Microsoft Copilot is listed for UCL in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: officially endorsed.

The three categories are guidance for communicating assessment expectations. Assessment briefs take precedence; staff may specify additional conditions, and individual assistive-technology exemptions must be clarified.
UCL designates Microsoft Copilot as its approved GenAI tool due to its enhanced data protection, positioning it as a more secure alternative to other GenAI services.
UCL defines academic misconduct in the context of GenAI as gaining an unfair advantage over other students; there is no single list of fair and unfair uses as it depends on the assessment category.
UCL provides Studiosity, a GenAI-powered service available 24/7 to all current students at all levels of study, to support academic writing and referencing skills.

UCL generally permits language and writing review that does not determine substantive content, subject to the assessment brief and assessed-language exceptions. CLIE Modern Foreign Language modules prohibit third-party or software language and writing review.

UCL Library guidance requires acknowledgement where GenAI has functionally contributed to the creation of academic work (e.g. drafting, planning, structuring), subject to discipline and assessment instructions. Minimum acknowledgement includes tool name and version, publisher, URL, and single-sentence context of use. Prompts, generation dates, and tracked-changes are additional requirements that apply only when stipulated by departments or assignment briefs. Preparatory reading, search summaries, and basic grammar assistance may not require acknowledgement. While UCL advises treating AI output as a work with no author, students and researchers must follow required departmental guidelines and standardised referencing styles (such as APA or Chicago), which may require citing the GenAI tool as an author.

UCL Press permits certain responsible supporting uses of GenAI in book preparation (brainstorming, language improvement, structure), subject to human oversight, accountability, and disclosure via the Gen AI Disclosure Form. GenAI tools cannot be credited as authors on research-based works. For research monographs, UCL Press does not permit GenAI creation or manipulation of images, figures, charts, tables, or original research data. Editors and peer reviewers shouldn't upload proposals or manuscripts into GenAI tools (advisory guidance), in contrast to the strict mandatory ban for UCL Press journals.

UCL Press journals prohibit listing AI as an author on research-based works. Broadly, AI use in creating, editing, or manipulating images or figures is not accepted; however, an explicit exception permits AI-assisted technologies used as part of research design or methodology (e.g. data visualisation to generate or interpret underlying data), provided it is fully declared and documented in the methodology. Editors and peer reviewers are strictly prohibited from submitting manuscripts or data reported in them through AI tools.

UCL does not invest in GenAI detection software. Staff must not submit student work into GenAI detection tools or GenAI services themselves, as this compromises students' intellectual property and personal data rights. Furthermore, due to lack of evidence that GenAI can mark effectively and without bias, staff should not use GenAI to mark student work. UCL markers do not use AI detector scores to establish academic misconduct. Initial informal discussions do not replace the formal Student Academic Misconduct Procedure; suspected inappropriate GenAI use or authorship issues may proceed through Stage 1 and an Investigatory Viva.

For an Investigatory Viva, the Secretary must supply the invitation, report and evidence at least five working days beforehand. Attendance is mandatory and the viva cannot be held in the student’s absence. Organisation should occur within 20 working days of the Stage 1 outcome unless reasonable circumstances prevent this. Stage 3 appeals must be submitted within 10 working days of receiving formal notification. Outcomes are normally issued within 20 working days after eligibility notification, with recommendations subject to Exam Board confirmation.

The March 2024 UCL Copilot announcement describes protected prompts, no saved chat and no model training when signed in with UCL credentials. These are dated source statements, not verification of current tenant settings. It advises staff not to enter personal, confidential or special-category data and to use content for which they have copyright.

CLIE oral and invigilated in-person assessments are Category 1 unless otherwise stated; non-invigilated written assessments are Category 2 with assistive use only. CLIE Modern Foreign Language modules prohibit language and writing review. Summer School rules are set by the teaching department. CLIE requires acknowledgement of GenAI use.

Doctoral candidates must list functional external contributions beyond their supervisory team in the Doctoral Candidate Thesis Declaration Form. GenAI drafting, including copyediting rather than proofreading, must be declared. Candidates retain responsibility and critical oversight, and examiners must be able to confirm satisfactory viva answers without AI support.

While UCL advises treating AI output as a work with no author, students and researchers must follow required departmental guidelines and standardised referencing styles (such as APA or Chicago), which may require citing the GenAI tool as an author.

UCL Press permits certain responsible supporting uses of GenAI in book preparation (brainstorming, language improvement, structure), subject to human oversight, accountability, and disclosure via the Gen AI Disclosure Form. GenAI tools cannot be credited as authors on research-based works. For research monographs, UCL Press does not permit GenAI creation or manipulation of images, figures, charts, tables, or original research data. Editors and peer reviewers shouldn't upload proposals or manuscripts into GenAI tools (advisory guidance), in contrast to the strict mandatory ban for UCL Press journals.

UCL Press journals prohibit listing AI as an author on research-based works. Broadly, AI use in creating, editing, or manipulating images or figures is not accepted; however, an explicit exception permits AI-assisted technologies used as part of research design or methodology (e.g. data visualisation to generate or interpret underlying data), provided it is fully declared and documented in the methodology. Editors and peer reviewers are strictly prohibited from submitting manuscripts or data reported in them through AI tools.

UCL does not invest in GenAI detection software. Staff must not submit student work into GenAI detection tools or GenAI services themselves, as this compromises students' intellectual property and personal data rights. Furthermore, due to lack of evidence that GenAI can mark effectively and without bias, staff should not use GenAI to mark student work. UCL markers do not use AI detector scores to establish academic misconduct. Initial informal discussions do not replace the formal Student Academic Misconduct Procedure; suspected inappropriate GenAI use or authorship issues may proceed through Stage 1 and an Investigatory Viva.

For an Investigatory Viva, the Secretary must supply the invitation, report and evidence at least five working days beforehand. Attendance is mandatory and the viva cannot be held in the student’s absence. Organisation should occur within 20 working days of the Stage 1 outcome unless reasonable circumstances prevent this. Stage 3 appeals must be submitted within 10 working days of receiving formal notification. Outcomes are normally issued within 20 working days after eligibility notification, with recommendations subject to Exam Board confirmation.

The March 2024 UCL Copilot announcement describes protected prompts, no saved chat and no model training when signed in with UCL credentials. These are dated source statements, not verification of current tenant settings. It advises staff not to enter personal, confidential or special-category data and to use content for which they have copyright.

CLIE oral and invigilated in-person assessments are Category 1 unless otherwise stated; non-invigilated written assessments are Category 2 with assistive use only. CLIE Modern Foreign Language modules prohibit language and writing review. Summer School rules are set by the teaching department. CLIE requires acknowledgement of GenAI use.

Doctoral candidates must list functional external contributions beyond their supervisory team in the Doctoral Candidate Thesis Declaration Form. GenAI drafting, including copyediting rather than proofreading, must be declared. Candidates retain responsibility and critical oversight, and examiners must be able to confirm satisfactory viva answers without AI support.

claimChanges.claimText: For the Fall 2027 application cycle, Caltech requires all applicants to review its ethical-use-of-AI guidelines before submitting supplemental essays. Noncompliance with those guidelines may result in rescission of admission. This is an admissions requirement for applicants, not a coursework rule or an automatic sanction for enrolled students.

Caltech IMSS lists its Windows 11 Copilot service as available and free. The official table labels that entry “Microsoft 365 Copilot for Windows 11”; this is kept as the source’s original label and does not establish availability of the separate Microsoft 365 Copilot for Education service.

Caltech admissions prohibits applicants from copying and pasting directly from an AI generator, relying on AI-generated content to outline or draft essays, replacing their unique voice with AI-generated content, or translating essays via AI.

Caltech admissions permits applicants to use AI tools like Grammarly or Microsoft Editor for grammar and spelling review of completed essays, to generate brainstorming questions or exercises, and to research the college application process.

Anthropic Claude Premium is listed for California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Anthropic Claude Standard is listed for California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: conditionally allowed. Derived endorsement type: institutionally licensed or procured.

Microsoft Copilot Web is listed for California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: officially endorsed.
Zoom AI Companion is listed for California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in an official university AI tools source. Derived availability: allowed. Derived endorsement type: officially endorsed.

In Caltech's Humanities and Social Sciences (HSS) division, students may use generative AI tools only in ways explicitly allowed by the course instructor in the course materials. Any usage not specifically allowed should be assumed to be disallowed.
The Caltech HSS generative AI policy applies to all assignments including major papers, exams, discussion board posts, reflections, and problem sets.
Caltech HSS students are expected to follow specific course guidance for documenting any permitted use of generative AI tools.

Caltech states that academic AI-use policies for enrolled students are determined by individual departments and/or faculty. Institutional IMSS security and data-governance standards also apply to Caltech-data workloads; departmental autonomy does not establish that no university-wide rules exist.
The Caltech HSS generative AI policy states that generative AI may promote learning in some contexts and impede it in others, and instructors prioritize student learning in setting these policies.

IMSS guidance prohibits restricted or confidential Caltech information in consumer AI tools. The LLM Standards permit a specific IMSS exception with compensating controls; catalogue access alone does not establish sensitive-data approval.

Generative AI platforms are strictly not approved for long-term storage, official records management, or institutional data retention; all records requiring retention must be stored in approved Caltech systems.

All generative AI usage at Caltech should adhere to four institutional principles: prompt disclosure or referencing of GenAI tools and application plug-ins as applicable, data and information protection, content responsibility by the user, and the Caltech Honor Code. This guidance does not mandate a universal prompt-log format or tool-version record.

For Caltech-data workloads, primary LLM inference must use Amazon Bedrock or other IMSS-approved platforms with no provider training on Caltech prompts/data, and custom training/fine-tuning must be performed on Amazon SageMaker or IMSS-approved secured environments.
Public, consumer, or unsanctioned GenAI tools are prohibited for Restricted or Confidential Caltech data unless IMSS issues a specific exception with compensating controls.

All AI traffic with Caltech data must use private networking (for example VPC Endpoints/PrivateLink or Direct Connect), with encryption in transit and at rest (TLS 1.2+; KMS CMKs). The examples are not an exclusive network list. Exceptions require Research Compliance Officer, CIO and CISO (or delegate) approval, compensating controls and an agreed sunset date.

AI agents operating in Caltech environments must be restricted to approved tools with explicit scopes and least-privilege credentials, and production tools must not allow arbitrary code execution without sandboxing.
LLM usage involving human subjects or protected research data must receive prior Institutional Review Board (IRB) and IMSS data-use review.
External LLM vendors (non-AWS) must execute a Security & Data Processing Addendum that explicitly prohibits provider model training on Caltech data.

Violations may result in access revocation, removal of workloads and disciplinary actions per Caltech IMSS. Persistent violations are escalated to the CIO, CISO, OGC and appropriate governance bodies.

Undergraduate respondents offered the Early Resolution Option have 7 calendar days to decide whether to accept responsibility and waive a full Board of Control hearing, and may seek the support of a trained community advisor.

Students with disabilities in handbook processes may request reasonable accommodation from CASS. Complaint details need not be disclosed except insofar as they assist determination. Arrangements are individual and must be requested in a timely manner.

Respondents in conduct proceedings have the right to an advisor from the Caltech community (who may not be an attorney); Student Affairs staff, Board of Control representatives, and Conduct Review Committee members are trained to serve as advisors.

Caltech Undergraduate and Graduate Deans, CTLO, and the Hixon Writing Center strongly discourage the use of AI-detection tools for student writing due to false positives, false negatives, bias, and unreliability.
For Caltech Bi 1 (2026), generative AI tools (such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and Colab AI) are prohibited unless an assignment explicitly instructs students to engage with them on a per-problem basis.
Caltech admissions advises applicants that a good rule of thumb for generative AI is that if a trusted adult shouldn't do it, AI shouldn't do it either.

Under the Caltech Honor System, the Dean of Graduate Studies reviews graduate coursework violations (consulting the Graduate Honor Council), while allegations of research misconduct are handled separately by the Office of Research Compliance (ORC).

Microsoft 365 Copilot for Education is listed in the official Caltech IMSS AI tools catalog as Coming Soon at $216/user/year via PTA order in access.caltech; it is not yet available as a live verified campus service.

The Caltech HSS generative AI policy states that generative AI may promote learning in some contexts and impede it in others, and instructors prioritize student learning in setting these policies.

IMSS guidance prohibits restricted or confidential Caltech information in consumer AI tools. The LLM Standards permit a specific IMSS exception with compensating controls; catalogue access alone does not establish sensitive-data approval.

Generative AI platforms are strictly not approved for long-term storage, official records management, or institutional data retention; all records requiring retention must be stored in approved Caltech systems.

All generative AI usage at Caltech should adhere to four institutional principles: prompt disclosure or referencing of GenAI tools and application plug-ins as applicable, data and information protection, content responsibility by the user, and the Caltech Honor Code. This guidance does not mandate a universal prompt-log format or tool-version record.

For Caltech-data workloads, primary LLM inference must use Amazon Bedrock or other IMSS-approved platforms with no provider training on Caltech prompts/data, and custom training/fine-tuning must be performed on Amazon SageMaker or IMSS-approved secured environments.
Public, consumer, or unsanctioned GenAI tools are prohibited for Restricted or Confidential Caltech data unless IMSS issues a specific exception with compensating controls.

All AI traffic with Caltech data must use private networking (for example VPC Endpoints/PrivateLink or Direct Connect), with encryption in transit and at rest (TLS 1.2+; KMS CMKs). The examples are not an exclusive network list. Exceptions require Research Compliance Officer, CIO and CISO (or delegate) approval, compensating controls and an agreed sunset date.

AI agents operating in Caltech environments must be restricted to approved tools with explicit scopes and least-privilege credentials, and production tools must not allow arbitrary code execution without sandboxing.
LLM usage involving human subjects or protected research data must receive prior Institutional Review Board (IRB) and IMSS data-use review.
External LLM vendors (non-AWS) must execute a Security & Data Processing Addendum that explicitly prohibits provider model training on Caltech data.

Violations may result in access revocation, removal of workloads and disciplinary actions per Caltech IMSS. Persistent violations are escalated to the CIO, CISO, OGC and appropriate governance bodies.

Undergraduate respondents offered the Early Resolution Option have 7 calendar days to decide whether to accept responsibility and waive a full Board of Control hearing, and may seek the support of a trained community advisor.

Students with disabilities in handbook processes may request reasonable accommodation from CASS. Complaint details need not be disclosed except insofar as they assist determination. Arrangements are individual and must be requested in a timely manner.

Respondents in conduct proceedings have the right to an advisor from the Caltech community (who may not be an attorney); Student Affairs staff, Board of Control representatives, and Conduct Review Committee members are trained to serve as advisors.

Caltech Undergraduate and Graduate Deans, CTLO, and the Hixon Writing Center strongly discourage the use of AI-detection tools for student writing due to false positives, false negatives, bias, and unreliability.
For Caltech Bi 1 (2026), generative AI tools (such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and Colab AI) are prohibited unless an assignment explicitly instructs students to engage with them on a per-problem basis.
Caltech admissions advises applicants that a good rule of thumb for generative AI is that if a trusted adult shouldn't do it, AI shouldn't do it either.

Under the Caltech Honor System, the Dean of Graduate Studies reviews graduate coursework violations (consulting the Graduate Honor Council), while allegations of research misconduct are handled separately by the Office of Research Compliance (ORC).

Microsoft 365 Copilot for Education is listed in the official Caltech IMSS AI tools catalog as Coming Soon at $216/user/year via PTA order in access.caltech; it is not yet available as a live verified campus service.

HKU states that researchers should clearly disclose generative AI tool usage in research outputs, publications, and presentations, including the type of GenAI used, data sources, and potential limitations.

HKU states that input data used with generative AI should comply with data protection laws and university policies, and that users should avoid sharing sensitive, confidential, or proprietary information with GenAI platforms.

HKU holds researchers responsible for the outputs generated by generative AI and their implications; GenAI should be used as a support tool, not a substitute for critical analysis and human expertise.
HKU states that researchers should ensure generative AI use does not infringe existing intellectual property rights or compromise research output ownership.
HKU's GenAI research guidelines are positioned as an institutional policy under the Research Integrity framework, approved by Senate in September 2025.

HKU permits GenAI for research ideation and background research only with documentation and acknowledgement, verification of accuracy, fairness and originality, fair representation and citation of primary sources, and protection against inevitable disclosure of patentable inventions.

HKU allows GenAI for experimentation, data collection and analysis only with documentation, fit-for-purpose and data verification, participant confidentiality and prior consent for disclosure beyond the study, protection of proprietary or agreement-controlled data, and applicable ethics-approved participant information for ultra-realistic generated materials.
HKU permits GenAI-generated research code only with documented and acknowledged use, verification of algorithms and software, and adequate testing that is conducted and reported.

Researchers lacking the training to verify algorithms, source code and software tests should not use GenAI to generate research code; they should collaborate with researchers who can take responsibility for the software and analysis.
In general, HKU does not allow GenAI-generated text or figures that constitute interpretation of research findings. Unavoidable use should be limited in scope, acknowledged and reported.

HKU requires the specific use of GenAI in the research process to be duly documented and acknowledged, in addition to citing human authors of published work. Authors remain responsible for all statements and claims in research outputs.

GenAI language editing and translation of author-written text are generally acceptable at HKU, subject to review, accuracy and bias checks and publisher acknowledgement rules. Direct or extensive GenAI use in thesis writing without significant human input is not allowed.

GenAI enhancement of research figures containing primary data is acceptable only if it does not alter interpretation. AI-generated images or other data should not be misrepresented as experimental data.
HKU does not accept use of GenAI in peer review of research outputs or funding applications because of integrity and confidentiality concerns.

Students and research assistants should seek supervisor approval for planned research use of GenAI and document the use. Research students should declare and specify such use at thesis submission for examination.

HKU TALIC guidance requires teachers to clearly communicate acceptable AI use for course activities and assessed assignments. Instructors decide how to integrate AI; institutional tool access does not determine permission for a particular assessment.

HKU TALIC guidance identifies misuse of AI or misrepresentation of AI work as independent creative work as violations of HKU regulations, with referral to the university disciplinary committee. This statement does not establish an automatic sanction.

HKU Faculty of Law requires students to declare AI use on its assignment cover sheet where a teacher permits it for an assignment; failure to declare is treated as academic misconduct akin to plagiarism.

For HKU Faculty of Law assessed work, an educative response may involve rewriting and resubmission with a penalty. Where this is not appropriate, an academic response may reduce the mark or give zero. Misuse may also be referred as a disciplinary offence; this is not automatic expulsion.

HKU GenAI App and API users who use personal data are responsible for obtaining explicit consent from data subjects, masking data and complying with applicable data-protection governance. Users are strictly advised against sharing PII or confidential University information in web-search-enabled prompts.
